Main.sentence: Civil rights movements are a worldwide series of ___E:political movements U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_movement)___ for ___E:equality before the law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equality_before_the_law)___ , that peaked in the 1960s. [citation needed] In many situations they have been characterized by ___E:nonviolent protests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolence)___ , or have taken the form of campaigns of ___E:civil resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_resistance)___ aimed at achieving change through ___E:nonviolent forms of resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent_resistance)___ .
In some situations, they have been accompanied, or followed, by ___E:civil unrest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_unrest)___ and armed rebellion.

The process has been long and tenuous in many countries, and many of these movements did not, or have yet to, fully achieve their goals, although the efforts of these movements have led to improvements in the legal rights of some previously oppressed groups of people, in some places.

The main aim of the successful ___E:civil rights movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement)___ and other social movements for civil rights included ensuring that the rights of all people were and are equally protected by the law. These include but are not limited to the ___E:rights of minorities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_rights)___ , ___E:women's rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_rights)___ , ___E:disability rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_rights)___ and ___E:LGBT rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights)___ .

___E:Northern Ireland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland)___ is a part of the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom)___ which has witnessed violence over many decades, known as ___E:the Troubles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles)___ , arising from tensions between the British ( ___E:Unionist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unionism_(Ireland))___ , Protestant) majority and the Irish ( ___E:Nationalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalism_(Ireland))___ , Catholic) minority following the ___E:Partition of Ireland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_Ireland)___ in 1920.

The civil rights struggle in Northern Ireland can be traced to activists in Dungannon, led by ___E:Austin Currie U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_Currie)___ , who were fighting for equal access to public housing for the members of the Catholic community.

This domestic issue would not have led to a fight for civil rights were it not for the fact that being a registered householder was a qualification for local government ___E:franchise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffrage)___ in Northern Ireland. [citation needed]
In January 1964, the ___E:Campaign for Social Justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_for_Social_Justice)___ (CSJ) was launched in Belfast.
This organisation joined the struggle for better housing and committed itself to ending discrimination in employment.
The CSJ promised the Catholic community that their cries would be heard.
They challenged the government and promised that they would take their case to the Commission for Human Rights in Strasbourg and to the United Nations.

Having started with basic domestic issues, the civil rights struggle in Northern Ireland escalated to a full-scale movement that found its embodiment in the ___E:Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Civil_Rights_Association)___ .

NICRA campaigned in the late sixties and early seventies, consciously modelling itself on the American civil rights movement and using similar methods of ___E:civil resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_resistance)___ .
NICRA organised marches and protests to demand equal rights and an end to discrimination.
NICRA originally had five main demands:
All of these specific demands were aimed at an ultimate goal that had been the one of women at the very beginning: the end of discrimination.
Civil rights activists all over Northern Ireland soon launched a campaign of ___E:civil resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_resistance)___ .

There was opposition from Loyalists, who were aided by the ___E:Royal Ulster Constabulary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Ulster_Constabulary)___ (RUC), Northern Ireland's police force. [citation needed] At this point, the RUC was over 90% Protestant.

Violence escalated, resulting in the rise of the ___E:Provisional Irish Republican Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army)___ (IRA) from the Catholic community, a group reminiscent of those from the War of Independence and the Civil War that occurred in the 1920s that had launched a campaign of violence to end British rule in Northern Ireland.

Loyalist ___E:paramilitaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitaries)___ countered this with a defensive campaign of violence and the ___E:British government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_government)___ responded with a policy of ___E:internment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment)___ without trial of suspected IRA members.
For more than 300 people, the internment lasted several years.
The huge majority of those interned by the British forces were Catholic.

In 1978, in a case brought by the government of the ___E:Republic of Ireland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland)___ against the government of the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom)___ , the ___E:European Court of Human Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights)___ ruled that the ___E:interrogation techniques U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_techniques)___ approved for use by British interrogators on internees in Northern Ireland amounted to "inhuman and degrading" treatment.
The IRA encouraged Republicans to join in the movement for civil rights but never controlled NICRA.
The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association fought for the end of discrimination toward Catholics and did not take a position on the legitimacy of the state.
Republican leader ___E:Gerry Adams U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerry_Adams)___ explained subsequently that Catholics saw that it was possible for them to have their demands heard.
He wrote that "we were able to see an example of the fact that you didn't just have to take it, you could fight back".

For an account and critique of the movements for civil rights in Northern Ireland, reflecting on the ambiguous link between the causes of civil rights and opposition to the union with the United Kingdom, see the work of Richard English.

One of the most important events in the era of civil rights in Northern Ireland took place in ___E:Derry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derry)___ , which escalated the conflict from peaceful civil disobedience to armed conflict.

The ___E:Battle of the Bogside U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Bogside)___ started on 12 August when an Apprentice Boys, a Protestant order, parade passed through Waterloo Place, where a large crowd was gathered at the mouth of William Street, on the edge of the Bogside.

Different accounts describe the first outbreak of violence, with reports stating that it was either an attack by youth from the ___E:Bogside U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogside)___ on the RUC, or fighting broke out between Protestants and Catholics.
The violence escalated and barricades were erected.
Proclaiming this district to be the ___E:Free Derry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Derry)___ , Bogsiders carried on fights with the RUC for days using stones and petrol bombs.

The government finally withdrew the RUC and ___E:replaced it U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Banner)___ with the ___E:British Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army)___ , which disbanded the crowds of Catholics who were barricaded in the Bogside.
___E:Bloody Sunday U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloody_Sunday_(1972))___ , 30 January 1972, in Derry is seen by some as a turning point in the movement for civil rights.

Fourteen unarmed Catholic civil rights marchers protesting against ___E:internment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment)___ were shot and killed by soldiers from the ___E:Parachute Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute_Regiment_(United_Kingdom))___ .
The peace process has made significant gains in recent years.
Through open dialogue from all parties, a state of ceasefire by all major paramilitary groups has lasted.
A stronger economy improved Northern Ireland's standard of living.

Civil rights issues have become less of a concern for many in Northern Ireland over the past 20 years as laws and policies protecting their rights, and forms of affirmative action, have been implemented for all government offices and many private businesses.
Tensions still exist, but the vast majority of citizens are no longer affected by violence.

The 1960s brought intense political and social change to the ___E:Canadian province U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_and_territories_of_Canada)___ of ___E:Quebec U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec)___ , with the election of Liberal Premier ___E:Jean Lesage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Lesage)___ after the death of ___E:Maurice Duplessis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Duplessis)___ , whose government was widely viewed as corrupt.

These changes included ___E:secularization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularization)___ of the education and health care systems, which were both heavily controlled by the ___E:Roman Catholic Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church)___ , whose support for Duplessis and his ___E:perceived corruption U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duplessis_Orphans)___ had angered many Québécois.

Policies of the Liberal government also sought to give Quebec more economic autonomy, such as the ___E:nationalization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalization)___ of ___E:Hydro-Québec U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydro-Qu%C3%A9bec)___ and the creation of public companies for the mining, forestry, iron/steel and petroleum industries of the province.
Other changes included the creation of the Régie des Rentes du Québec (Quebec Pension Plan) and new labour codes that made unionizing easier and gave workers the right to strike.

The social and economic changes of the Quiet Revolution gave life to the ___E:Quebec sovereignty movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_sovereignty_movement)___ , as more and more Québécois saw themselves as a distinctly culturally different from the rest of Canada.

The segregationist ___E:Parti Québécois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parti_Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois)___ was created in 1968 and won the ___E:1976 Quebec general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Quebec_general_election)___ .

They enacted ___E:legislation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_101)___ meant to enshrine ___E:French U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language)___ as the language of business in the province, while also controversially restricting the usage of ___E:English U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language)___ on signs and restricting the eligibility of students to be taught in English.

A radical strand of ___E:French Canadian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Canadian)___ nationalism produced the ___E:Front de libération du Québec U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_de_lib%C3%A9ration_du_Qu%C3%A9bec)___ (FLQ), which since 1963 has been using ___E:terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism)___ to make ___E:Quebec U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec)___ a sovereign nation.

In October 1970, in response to the arrest of some of its members earlier in the year, the FLQ kidnapped British diplomat ___E:James Cross U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cross)___ and Quebec's Minister of Labour ___E:Pierre Laporte U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Laporte)___ , whom they later killed.

The then Canadian Prime Minister ___E:Pierre Elliott Trudeau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Elliott_Trudeau)___ , himself a French Canadian, invoked the ___E:War Measures Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Measures_Act)___ , declared ___E:martial law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law)___ in Quebec, and arrested the kidnappers by the end of the year.

Movements for civil rights in the United States include noted legislation and organized efforts to abolish public and private acts of ___E:racial discrimination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_discrimination)___ against ___E:African Americans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American)___ and other disadvantaged groups between 1954 and 1968, particularly in the ___E:southern United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States)___ .
It is sometimes referred to as the Second Reconstruction era, alluding to the unresolved issues of the ___E:Reconstruction Era U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_Era)___ (1863–1877).

After 1890, the system of ___E:Jim Crow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow)___ , disenfranchisement, and second class citizenship degraded the citizenship rights of African Americans, especially in the South.
It was the ___E:nadir of American race relations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadir_of_American_race_relations)___ .

There were three main aspects: ___E:racial segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation)___ – upheld by the ___E:United States Supreme Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court)___ decision in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 –, legally mandated by southern governments—voter suppression or ___E:disfranchisement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disfranchisement)___ in the southern states, and private acts of violence and ___E:mass racial violence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_racial_violence_in_the_United_States)___ aimed at African Americans, unhindered or encouraged by government authorities.

Although racial discrimination was present nationwide, the combination of law, public and private acts of discrimination, marginal economic opportunity, and violence directed toward African Americans in the southern states became known as ___E:Jim Crow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws)___ .

Noted strategies employed prior to 1955 included litigation and lobbying attempts by the ___E:National Association for the Advancement of Colored People U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People)___ (NAACP).
These efforts were a hallmark of the early American Civil Rights Movement from 1896 to 1954.
By 1955, blacks became frustrated by gradual approaches to implement desegregation by federal and state governments and the "massive resistance" by whites.

The black leadership adopted a combined strategy of ___E:direct action U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_action)___ with ___E:nonviolence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolence)___ , sometimes resulting in ___E:nonviolent resistance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolence)___ and ___E:civil disobedience U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience)___ .
Some of the acts of ___E:nonviolence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolence)___ and civil disobedience produced crisis situations between practitioners and government authorities.
The authorities of federal, state, and local governments often acted with an immediate response to end the crisis situations – sometimes in the practitioners' favor.

Some of the different forms of protests and/or civil disobedience employed included ___E:economic boycotts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycott)___ , as successfully practiced by the ___E:Montgomery bus boycott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery_bus_boycott)___ (1955–1956) in Alabama which gave the movement one of its more famous icons in ___E:Rosa Parks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_Parks)___ ; " ___E:sit-ins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sit-ins)___ ", as demonstrated by two influential events, the ___E:Greensboro sit-in U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greensboro_Four)___ (1960) in North Carolina and the ___E:Nashville sit-ins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_sit-ins)___ in Nashville, Tennessee; the influential ___E:1963 Birmingham Children's Crusade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birmingham_Campaign)___ , in which children were set upon by the local authorities with fire hoses and attack dogs, and longer marches, as exhibited by the ___E:Selma to Montgomery marches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selma_to_Montgomery_marches)___ (1965) in Alabama which at first was resisted and attacked by the state and local authorities, and resulted in the ___E:1965 Voting Rights Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Voting_Rights_Act)___ .
The evidence of changing attitudes could also be seen around the country, where small businesses sprang up supporting the Civil Rights Movement, such as New Jersey's Everybody's Luncheonette.

Besides the Children's Crusade and the ___E:Selma to Montgomery marches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selma_to_Montgomery_marches)___ , another illustrious event of the 1960s Civil Rights Movement was the ___E:March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Washington_for_Jobs_and_Freedom)___ in August, 1963. It is best remembered for the " ___E:I Have a Dream U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Have_a_Dream)___ " speech by ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ in which the speech turned into a national text and eclipsed the troubles the organizers had to bring to march forward.
It had been a fairly complicated affair to bring together various leaders of civil rights, religious and labor groups.
As the name of the march implies, many compromises had to be made in order to unite the followers of so many different causes.

The "March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom" emphasized the combined purposes of the march and the goals that each of the leaders aimed at. The 1963 March on Washington organizers and organizational leaders, informally named the " ___E:Big Six U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Six_(activists))___ ", were ___E:A. Philip Randolph U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Philip_Randolph)___ , ___E:Roy Wilkins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Wilkins)___ , ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ , ___E:Whitney Young U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Young)___ , ___E:James Farmer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Farmer)___ and ___E:John Lewis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis)___ .

Although they came from different backgrounds and political interests, these organizers and leaders were intent on the peacefulness of the march, which had its own marshal to ensure that the event would be peaceful and respectful of the law.  The success of the march is still being debated, but one aspect which has been raised was the misrepresentation of women.

A lot of feminine civil rights groups had participated in the organization of the march, but when it came to actual activity women were denied the right to speak and were relegated to figurative roles in the back of the stage.

As some female participants noticed, the March can be remembered for the "I Have a Dream" speech but for some female activists it was a new awakening, forcing black women not only to fight for civil rights but also to engage in the Feminist movement.

Noted achievements of the ___E:Civil Rights Movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Movement)___ include the judicial victory in the Brown v. Board of Education case that nullified the legal article of " ___E:separate but equal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separate_but_equal)___ " and made segregation legally impermissible, and the passages of the ___E:1964 Civil Rights Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Civil_Rights_Act)___ , .  that banned discrimination in employment practices and public accommodations, passage of the ___E:Voting Rights Act of 1965 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voting_Rights_Act_of_1965)___ that restored voting rights, and passage of the ___E:Civil Rights Act of 1968 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1968)___ that banned discrimination in the sale or rental of housing.

By 1967 the emergence of the ___E:Black Power movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Power_movement)___ (1966–75) began to gradually eclipse the original " ___E:integrated power U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_integration)___ " aims of the successful Civil Rights Movement that had been espoused by ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ and others.

Advocates of Black Power argued for black ___E:self-determination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-determination)___ , and asserted that the ___E:assimilation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_assimilation)___ inherent in integration robs ___E:Africans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Africanism)___ of their common heritage and dignity.

For example, the theorist and activist ___E:Omali Yeshitela U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omali_Yeshitela)___ argues that Africans have historically fought to protect their lands, cultures, and freedoms from European ___E:colonialists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialism)___ , and that any integration into the society which has stolen another people and their wealth is an act of ___E:treason U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treason)___ .

Today, most Black Power advocates have not changed their self-sufficiency argument. ___E:Racism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism)___ still exists worldwide, and some believe that blacks in the United States, on the whole, did not assimilate into U.S. "mainstream" culture.

Blacks arguably became even more oppressed, this time partially by "their own" people in a new black ___E:stratum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_stratification)___ of the ___E:middle class U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_class)___ and the ___E:ruling class U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruling_class)___ .

Black Power's advocates generally argue that the reason for this ___E:stalemate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalemate)___ and further oppression of the vast majority of U.S. blacks is because Black Power's objectives have not had the opportunity to be fully carried through.

One of the most public manifestations of the Black Power movement took place in the 1968 Olympics, when two African-Americans, ___E:Tommie Smith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommie_Smith)___ and ___E:John Carlos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carlos)___ , stood on the podium doing a Black Power salute.
This act is still remembered today as the ___E:1968 Olympics Black Power salute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Olympics_Black_Power_salute)___ .
The Chicano Movement occurred during the civil rights era that sought political empowerment and social inclusion for Mexican-Americans around a generally nationalist argument.
The Chicano movement blossomed in the 1960s and was active through the late 1970s in various regions of the U.S.
The movement had roots in the civil rights struggles that had preceded it, adding to it the cultural and generational politics of the era.

The early heroes of the movement— ___E:Rodolfo Gonzales U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodolfo_Gonzales)___ in ___E:Denver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver)___ and ___E:Reies Tijerina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reies_Tijerina)___ in New Mexico—adopted a historical account of the preceding hundred and twenty-five years that had obscured much of Mexican-American history.

Gonzales and Tijerina embraced a nationalism that identified the failure of the United States government to live up to its promises in the ___E:Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Guadalupe_Hidalgo)___ .

In that account, Mexican Americans were a conquered people who simply needed to reclaim their birthright and cultural heritage as part of a new nation, which later became known as ___E:Aztlán U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztl%C3%A1n)___ .
That version of the past did not, but take into account the history of those Mexicans who had immigrated to the United States.

It also gave little attention to the rights of undocumented immigrants in the United States in the 1960s— which is not surprising, since immigration did not have the political significance it later acquired.
It was a decade later when activists, such as Bert Corona in California, embraced the rights of undocumented workers and helped broaden the movement to include their issues.

When the movement dealt with practical problems in the 1960s, most activists focused on the most immediate issues confronting Mexican Americans; unequal educational and employment opportunities, political disfranchisement, and police brutality.

In the heady days of the late 1960s, when the student movement was active around the globe, the Chicano movement brought about more or less spontaneous actions, such as the mass walkouts by high school students in Denver and ___E:East Los Angeles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Los_Angeles,_California)___ in 1968 and the ___E:Chicano Moratorium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicano_Moratorium)___ in Los Angeles in 1970.

The movement was particularly strong at the college level, where activists formed MEChA, Movimiento Estudiantil Chicano de Aztlán , which promoted Chicano Studies programs and a generalized ethno-nationalist agenda.

At a time when peaceful ___E:sit-ins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sit-in)___ were a common protest tactic, the ___E:American Indian Movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Indian_Movement)___ (AIM) takeovers in their early days were noticeably violent.
Some appeared to be spontaneous outcomes of protest gatherings, but others included armed seizure of public facilities.

The ___E:Alcatraz Island U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcatraz_Island)___ occupation of 1969, although commonly associated with NAM, pre-dated the organization, but was a catalyst for its formation.
In 1970, AIM occupied abandoned property at the ___E:Naval Air Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Air_Station)___ near ___E:Minneapolis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis)___ .
In July 1971, it assisted in a takeover of the Winter Dam, Lac Courte Oreilles, and ___E:Wisconsin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin)___ .

When activists took over the ___E:Bureau of Indian Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Indian_Affairs)___ Headquarters in Washington, D.C. in November 1972, they sacked the building and 24 people were arrested.
Activists occupied the ___E:Custer County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custer_County,_South_Dakota)___ Courthouse in 1973, though police routed the occupation after a riot took place.
In 1973 activists and military forces confronted each other in the ___E:Wounded Knee incident U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wounded_Knee_incident)___ .
The standoff lasted 71 days, and two men died in the violence.

If the period associated with ___E:first-wave feminism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-wave_feminism)___ focused upon absolute rights such as ___E:suffrage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage)___ (which led to women attaining the right to vote in the early part of the 20th century), the period of the ___E:second-wave feminism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-wave_feminism)___ was concerned with the issues such as changing social attitudes and economic, reproductive, and educational equality (including the ability to have careers in addition to motherhood, or the right to choose not to have children) between the genders and addressed the rights of female minorities.

The new feminist movement, which spanned from 1963 to 1982, explored economic equality, political power at all levels, professional equality, reproductive freedoms, issues with the family, educational equality, sexuality, and many other issues.

Since the mid-19th century in ___E:Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany)___ , social reformers have used the language of civil rights to argue against the oppression of same-sex sexuality, same-sex emotional intimacy, and ___E:gender variance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_variance)___ .

Largely, but not exclusively, these ___E:LGBT movements U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_movements)___ have characterized gender variant and homosexually oriented people as a ___E:minority group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_group)___ (s); this was the approach taken by the ___E:homophile movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophile_movement)___ of the 1940s, 1950s and early 1960s.

With the rise of ___E:secularism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularism)___ in the West, an increasing sexual openness, women's liberation, the 1960s ___E:counterculture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterculture_of_the_1960s)___ , the AIDS epidemic, and a range of ___E:new social movements U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_social_movements)___ , the homophile movement underwent a rapid growth and transformation, with a focus on building community and unapologetic activism which came to be known as the ___E:Gay Liberation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_Liberation)___ .

The words "Gay Liberation" echoed "Women's Liberation"; the ___E:Gay Liberation Front U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gay_Liberation_Front)___ consciously took its name from the "National Liberation Fronts" of ___E:Vietnam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Front_for_the_Liberation_of_Vietnam)___ and ___E:Algeria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algerian_National_Liberation_Front)___ , and the slogan "Gay Power", as a defiant answer to the rights-oriented homophile movement, was inspired by ___E:Black Power U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Power)___ and ___E:Chicano U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicano)___ Power.
The GLF's statement of purpose explained:
We are a revolutionary group of men and women formed with the realization that complete sexual liberation for all people cannot come about unless existing social institutions are abolished.
We reject society's attempt to impose sexual roles and definitions of our nature.
— GLF statement of purpose
GLF activist ___E:Martha Shelley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Shelley)___ wrote,
We are women and men who, from the time of our earliest memories, have been in revolt against the sex-role structure and nuclear family structure.
— "Gay is Good", ___E:Martha Shelley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Shelley)___ , 1970

Gay Liberationists aimed at transforming fundamental concepts and institutions of society, such as ___E:gender U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender)___ and the ___E:family U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family)___ .

In the 1960s, the early years of the ___E:Brezhnev stagnation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Era_of_Stagnation)___ , ___E:dissidents in the Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_dissidents)___ increasingly turned their attention civil and eventually human rights concerns.

The fight for civil and human rights focused on issues of ___E:freedom of expression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_the_Soviet_Union)___ , ___E:freedom of conscience U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Christians_in_the_Soviet_Union)___ , ___E:freedom to emigrate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refusenik)___ , ___E:punitive psychiatry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_abuse_of_psychiatry_in_the_Soviet_Union)___ , and the plight of ___E:political prisoners U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_repression_in_the_Soviet_Union)___ .
It was characterized by a new openness of dissent, a concern for legality, the rejection of any 'underground' and violent struggle.

It played a significant role in providing a common language and goal for many Soviet dissidents, and became a cause for diverse social groups in the dissident millieu, ranging from activists in the youth subculture to academics such as ___E:Andrei Sakhrarov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrei_Sakharov)___ .
Significantly, Soviet dissidents of the 1960s introduced the "legalist" approach of avoiding moral and political commentary in favor of close attention to legal and procedural issues.

Following several landmark trials of writers ( ___E:Sinyavsky-Daniel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinyavsky%E2%80%93Daniel_trial)___ trial, the trials of ___E:Alexander Ginzburg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Ginzburg)___ and ___E:Yuri Galanskov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Galanskov)___ ) and an associated crackdown on dissidents by the ___E:KGB U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KGB)___ , coverage of arrests and trials in ___E:samizdat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samizdat)___ (unsanctioned press) became more common.

This activity eventually led to the founding of the Chronicle of Current Events in April 1968. The unofficial newsletter reported violations of civil rights and judicial procedure by the Soviet government and responses to those violations by citizens across the USSR.

Throughout the 1960s–1980s, dissidents in the civil and human rights movement engaged in a variety of activities: The documentation of political repression and rights violations in ___E:samizdat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samizdat)___ (unsanctioned press); individual and collective protest letters and petitions; unsanctioned demonstrations; an informal network of mutual aid for prisoners of conscience; and, most prominently, civic watch groups appealing to the international community.

All of these activities came at great personal risk and with repercussions ranging from dismissal from work and studies to many years of imprisonment in ___E:labor camps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_camp)___ and being subjected to ___E:punitive psychiatry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_abuse_of_psychiatry_in_the_Soviet_Union)___ .
The rights-based strategy of dissent merged with the idea of human rights.

The human rights movement included figures such as ___E:Valery Chalidze U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valery_Chalidze)___ , ___E:Yuri Orlov U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Orlov)___ , and ___E:Lyudmila Alexeyeva U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyudmila_Alexeyeva)___ .

Special groups were founded such as the ___E:Initiative Group for the Defense of Human Rights in the USSR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initiative_Group_for_the_Defense_of_Human_Rights_in_the_USSR)___ (1969) and the ___E:Committee on Human Rights in the USSR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Committee_on_Human_Rights_in_the_USSR)___ (1970).

Though faced with the loss of many members to prisons, labor camps, psychiatric institutions and exile, they documented abuses, wrote appeals to international human rights bodies, collected signatures for petitions, and attended trials.

The signing of the ___E:Helsinki Accords U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_Accords)___ (1975) containing human rights clauses provided civil rights campaigners with a new hope to use international instruments.

This led to the creation of dedicated ___E:Helsinki Watch Groups U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki_Watch_Group)___ in Moscow ( ___E:Moscow Helsinki Group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow_Helsinki_Group)___ ), Kiev ( ___E:Ukrainian Helsinki Group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Helsinki_Group)___ ), Vilnius ( ___E:Lithuanian Helsinki Group U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_Helsinki_Group)___ ), Tbilisi, and Erevan (1976–77).  : 159–194

The Prague Spring ( ___E:Czech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_language)___ : Pražské jaro , ___E:Slovak U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovak_language)___ : Pražská jar , ___E:Russian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language)___ : пражская весна) was a period of political liberalization in ___E:Czechoslovakia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia)___ starting on January 5, 1968, and running until August 20 of that year, when the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ and its ___E:Warsaw Pact U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Pact)___ allies (except for ___E:Romania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania)___ ) invaded the country.

During ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , Czechoslovakia fell into the Soviet sphere of influence, the ___E:Eastern Bloc U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc)___ .

Since 1948 there were no parties other than the ___E:Communist Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_Czechoslovakia)___ in the country and it was indirectly managed by the Soviet Union.
Unlike other countries of Central and Eastern Europe, the communist take-over in Czechoslovakia in 1948 was, although as brutal as elsewhere, a genuine popular movement.
Reform in the country did not lead to the convulsions seen in ___E:Hungary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary)___ .

Towards the end of World War II ___E:Joseph Stalin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin)___ wanted Czechoslovakia, and signed an agreement with ___E:Winston Churchill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill)___ and ___E:Franklin D. Roosevelt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt)___ that ___E:Prague U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague)___ would be liberated by the ___E:Red Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army)___ , despite the fact that the ___E:United States Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army)___ under General ___E:George S. Patton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_S._Patton)___ could have liberated the city earlier.

This was important for the spread of pro-Russian (and pro-communist) ___E:propaganda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda)___ that came right after the war. People still remembered what they felt as Czechoslovakia's betrayal by the West at the ___E:Munich Agreement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement)___ .
For these reasons, the people voted for communists in the 1948 elections, the last democratic poll to take place there for a long time.
From the middle of the 1960s, Czechs and Slovaks showed increasing signs of rejection of the existing regime.
This change was reflected by reformist elements within the communist party by installing ___E:Alexander Dubček U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Dub%C4%8Dek)___ as party leader.

Dubček's reforms of the political process inside Czechoslovakia, which he referred to as Socialism with a human face , did not represent a complete overthrow of the old regime, as was the case in ___E:Hungary in 1956 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Hungarian_Revolution)___ .

Dubček's changes had broad support from the society, including the ___E:working class U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_class)___ , but was seen by the Soviet leadership as a threat to their hegemony over other states of the Eastern Bloc and to the very safety of the Soviet Union.

Czechoslovakia was in the middle of the defensive line of the Warsaw Pact and its possible defection to the enemy was unacceptable during the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ .

However, a sizeable minority in the ruling party, especially at higher leadership levels, was opposed to any lessening of the party's grip on society and actively plotted with the leadership of the Soviet Union to overthrow the reformers.
This group watched in horror as calls for multi-party elections and other reforms began echoing throughout the country.
Between the nights of August 20 and August 21, 1968, Eastern Bloc armies from five Warsaw Pact countries invaded Czechoslovakia.
During the invasion, Soviet tanks ranging in numbers from 5,000 to 7,000 occupied the streets.
They were followed by a large number of Warsaw Pact troops ranging from 200,000 to 600,000.

The Soviets insisted that they had been invited to invade the country, stating that loyal Czechoslovak Communists had told them that they were in need of "fraternal assistance against the ___E:counter-revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-revolution)___ ".
A letter which was found in 1989 proved an invitation to invade did indeed exist.

During the attack of the Warsaw Pact armies, 72 ___E:Czechs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechs)___ and ___E:Slovaks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovaks)___ were killed (19 of those in ___E:Slovakia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia)___ ) and hundreds were wounded (up to September 3, 1968).
Alexander Dubček called upon his people not to resist.
He was arrested and taken to ___E:Moscow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow)___ , along with several of his colleagues.
